questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A thick, continuous line in technical drawing is typically used to represent
options: the visible outline of an object
questions.explanation: Thick continuous lines represent the visible outlines and edges of an object, making them stand out clearly on the drawing.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A thin, continuous line in technical drawing is typically used for
options: the main visible outline of an object
dimension lines, extension lines, and projection lines
questions.explanation: Thin continuous lines are used for secondary information such as dimensioning, extension lines, and construction/projection lines, distinct from the bold outline.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A line made up of short dashes, used to represent edges or details hidden from the current view, is called a
questions.explanation: Hidden lines, drawn as a series of short dashes, indicate edges or features that are not visible from the current viewing angle.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A line made up of alternating long and short dashes, used to indicate the axis of symmetry or the centre of a circle, is called a
questions.explanation: Centre lines, drawn with a long-dash, short-dash pattern, mark axes of symmetry and the centres of circular features.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The process of dividing a line into two exactly equal parts using compass and straightedge construction is called
questions.explanation: Bisecting a line divides it precisely into two equal halves, typically achieved using compass arcs from each endpoint.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The process of dividing an angle into two exactly equal parts using compass and straightedge construction is called
questions.explanation: Bisecting an angle divides it into two equal smaller angles, constructed using compass arcs from the angle's vertex and sides.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Two lines that maintain a constant distance from each other and never meet, no matter how far extended, are called
questions.explanation: Parallel lines run in the same direction at a constant distance apart, never converging or crossing.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Two lines that meet each other at exactly 90 degrees are called
questions.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect to form a right angle (90 degrees) at their point of crossing.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A three-sided plane figure, whose interior angles always sum to 180 degrees, is called a
questions.explanation: A triangle is a three-sided polygon, with its interior angles always summing to exactly 180 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A four-sided plane figure with all sides equal in length and all angles equal to 90 degrees is called a
questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides and four right angles, making it a special case of both a rectangle and a rhombus.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A four-sided plane figure with opposite sides equal and parallel, and all angles equal to 90 degrees, but not all sides necessarily equal, is called a
questions.explanation: A rectangle has four right angles and equal opposite sides, but unlike a square, its adjacent sides are not necessarily equal.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A four-sided plane figure with all sides of equal length, but angles that are not necessarily 90 degrees, is called a
questions.explanation: A rhombus has four equal sides, but its angles can differ from 90 degrees, distinguishing it from a square.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular polygon with five equal sides and five equal angles is called a
questions.explanation: A regular pentagon has five equal sides and five equal interior angles, each measuring 108 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular polygon with six equal sides and six equal angles is called a
questions.explanation: A regular hexagon has six equal sides and six equal interior angles, each measuring 120 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular polygon with seven equal sides and seven equal angles is called a
questions.explanation: A regular heptagon has seven equal sides and seven equal interior angles.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular polygon with eight equal sides and eight equal angles is called an
questions.explanation: A regular octagon has eight equal sides and eight equal interior angles, each measuring 135 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The sum of the interior angles of any polygon with n sides can be calculated using the formula
questions.explanation: The interior angle sum formula, (n-2) x 180 degrees, applies to any simple polygon, allowing calculation for any number of sides.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When constructing a regular polygon given the length of one side, a common method involves first
options: dividing a circle into the required number of equal arcs corresponding to the polygon's sides
ignoring the given side length entirely
measuring only the diagonal of the polygon
drawing random lines with no defined angles
questions.explanation: A standard construction method involves dividing a circumscribing circle into equal arcs matching the number of sides needed, then connecting the resulting points.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A four-sided plane figure with only one pair of parallel sides is called a
questions.explanation: A trapezium (trapezoid) has exactly one pair of parallel sides, distinguishing it from parallelograms which have two pairs.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A triangle with all three sides of equal length is called an
questions.explanation: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal in length, and consequently all three interior angles equal to 60 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A circle passing through three given points can be constructed by finding the
options: midpoint of only one of the connecting lines
intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the lines joining the points
sum of the distances between the points
questions.explanation: The centre of a circle passing through three points lies at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the chords connecting those points.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point, without crossing into its interior, is called a
questions.explanation: A tangent line touches a circle at exactly one point and does not cross into the circle's interior.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A straight line segment joining two points on a circle's circumference, passing through the circle's interior, is called a
questions.explanation: A chord connects any two points on a circle's circumference, passing through the interior, unlike a tangent which only touches the circle at one point.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: An arc that connects two circles smoothly and touches each circle at exactly one point, without crossing either, is called an
questions.explanation: An arc of tangency smoothly bridges two circles or lines, maintaining a single point of contact with each without intersecting them.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When constructing a tangent arc that touches two circles externally (curving away from both), the arc's centre must be located at a distance from each circle's centre equal to
options: the sum of the tangent arc's radius and each circle's radius
exactly half of each circle's radius
the difference between the tangent arc's radius and each circle's radius
questions.explanation: For an external tangency arc, the distance from its centre to each circle's centre equals the tangent arc's radius plus that circle's own radius.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When constructing a tangent arc that touches two circles internally (curving around and enclosing part of them), the arc's centre must be located at a distance from each circle's centre equal to
options: the difference between the tangent arc's radius and each circle's radius
the sum of the tangent arc's radius and each circle's radius
questions.explanation: For an internal tangency arc, the distance from its centre to each circle's centre equals the tangent arc's radius minus that circle's own radius.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The path traced by a point that moves according to a specific geometric rule is called a
questions.explanation: A locus (plural: loci) is the path traced by a point moving under a defined geometric condition or rule.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: An oval-shaped curve traced by a point moving so that the sum of its distances from two fixed points (foci) remains constant is called an
questions.explanation: An ellipse is defined as the locus of points where the sum of the distances to two fixed foci is always constant.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A common method for constructing an ellipse using two concentric circles of different radii is called the
questions.explanation: The concentric circles method constructs an ellipse using two circles of major and minor axis radii, plotting points derived from their intersections.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: An alternative method for constructing an ellipse using a sliding strip marked with points corresponding to the major and minor axes is called the
questions.explanation: The trammel method uses a marked strip of card or paper, slid along guide lines, to plot points forming an accurate ellipse.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A curve traced by a point on the boundary of a circle as it rolls along a straight line without slipping is called a
questions.explanation: A cycloid is generated by tracking a point on a circle's circumference as the circle rolls along a straight line.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A curve formed by the locus of points equidistant from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed straight line (directrix) is called a
questions.explanation: A parabola is defined as the set of points equidistant from a fixed focus point and a fixed directrix line.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A spiral in which the distance from the centre increases by a constant amount for each equal angle of rotation is called an
questions.explanation: An Archimedean spiral expands at a constant rate outward from its centre with each full rotation, unlike spirals with an exponentially increasing rate.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A straight line passing through the centre of a circle and touching the circle at two opposite points is called a
questions.explanation: A diameter is a straight line passing through the centre of a circle, connecting two points on the circumference, and is twice the length of the radius.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A straight line from the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference is called a
questions.explanation: A radius connects the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference, and is half the length of the diameter.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Converting an irregular polygon into a triangle of equal area, using geometric construction, is generally achieved by
options: doubling the number of sides of the polygon
successively removing one vertex at a time while preserving the total area, until only a triangle remains
measuring the perimeter of the polygon only
randomly guessing an equivalent triangle shape
questions.explanation: The standard method reduces a polygon's number of sides one at a time through area-preserving constructions, until a triangle of equal area remains.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When reducing a quadrilateral to a triangle of equal area, a construction line is typically drawn
options: parallel to a diagonal, through the vertex to be eliminated, to a point on an extended side
outside the figure with no connection to its vertices
through the exact centre of the shape only
questions.explanation: A line drawn parallel to a diagonal, passing through the vertex to be removed, intersects an extended side at a point that preserves the original area when the vertex is eliminated.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Converting a triangle into a rectangle of equal area is a common technique used to
options: decrease the actual area of the original figure
eliminate the need for accurate measurement
increase the actual area of the original figure
simplify area comparison and calculation between differently shaped figures
questions.explanation: Converting shapes into simpler equivalent forms, like rectangles, makes it easier to visually compare or calculate areas of differently shaped figures.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The area of a triangle can be calculated using the formula
options: half of the base multiplied by the perpendicular height
the base multiplied by the hypotenuse
the base multiplied by the height
the sum of all three sides
questions.explanation: The area of a triangle equals half the product of its base length and its perpendicular height.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The area of a rectangle can be calculated using the formula
options: the sum of the length and width
half of the length multiplied by width
questions.explanation: The area of a rectangle is found by multiplying its length by its width.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The area of a regular polygon can generally be calculated using the formula
options: the diameter multiplied by the number of sides
the perimeter multiplied by the number of sides
half of the perimeter multiplied by the apothem (the distance from the centre to the midpoint of a side)
half of one side multiplied by the number of vertices
questions.explanation: The area of any regular polygon can be found using half the perimeter multiplied by the apothem, the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side's midpoint.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When converting a rectangle to a square of equal area, a common construction method uses
options: only the perimeter of the rectangle
a random estimate with no geometric construction
a semicircle drawn on the extended length, with the square's side found using the geometric mean
the sum of the length and width divided by two
questions.explanation: A classic construction converts a rectangle to an equal-area square by using a semicircle and the geometric mean relationship between the rectangle's length and width.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Reducing a complex irregular polygon to a rectangle of equal area is often done in two stages, first reducing the polygon to
options: a circle of equal area directly
a triangle of equal area, then converting that triangle to an equivalent rectangle
questions.explanation: The standard two-stage process first reduces an irregular polygon to an equivalent-area triangle, which is then converted into an equivalent-area rectangle.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing method that represents a three-dimensional object using multiple related two-dimensional views, such as front, end, and plan, is called
questions.explanation: Orthographic projection depicts an object through separate, related two-dimensional views, typically showing front, end, and plan elevations.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In orthographic projection, the view showing the object as seen directly from the front is called the
questions.explanation: The front elevation shows the object as viewed directly from the front, one of the three standard orthographic views.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In orthographic projection, the view showing the object as seen directly from the side is called the
questions.explanation: The end elevation shows the object as viewed directly from one side (end), complementing the front elevation and plan.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In orthographic projection, the view showing the object as seen directly from above is called the
questions.explanation: The plan view shows the object as seen directly from above, providing the top-down perspective in orthographic projection.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In First-Angle orthographic projection, the plan view is conventionally placed
options: beside the front elevation on the left only
questions.explanation: In First-Angle projection (the convention widely used in Europe and much of Africa), the plan view is drawn below the front elevation.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In Third-Angle orthographic projection, the plan view is conventionally placed
questions.explanation: In Third-Angle projection (the convention widely used in the United States), the plan view is drawn above the front elevation, opposite to First-Angle convention.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A pictorial drawing method that represents all three dimensions of an object using axes set at 30 degrees to the horizontal is called
questions.explanation: Isometric projection uses three axes, typically set 30 degrees from the horizontal, to represent an object's height, width, and depth in a single pictorial view.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A pictorial drawing method that shows one face of an object true to shape and size, with receding lines drawn at 45 degrees, is called
questions.explanation: Oblique projection keeps the front face of an object undistorted, with depth shown by receding lines typically drawn at 45 degrees.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: An oblique drawing in which the receding lines are drawn at full scale, matching the true depth of the object, is called a
questions.explanation: Cavalier oblique drawings show receding depth lines at full true length, though this can make the object appear distorted or exaggerated in depth.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: An oblique drawing in which the receding lines are drawn at half scale to reduce visual distortion is called a
questions.explanation: Cabinet oblique drawings halve the length of receding depth lines compared to cavalier oblique, producing a more realistic, less distorted appearance.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A pictorial drawing method that represents objects converging toward a single vanishing point on the horizon is called
questions.explanation: One-point perspective uses a single vanishing point on the horizon line, toward which all receding parallel lines converge.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A pictorial drawing method that represents objects converging toward two separate vanishing points on the horizon is called
questions.explanation: Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points on the horizon, giving a more dynamic and realistic representation of an object viewed at an angle.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The horizontal line representing eye level, toward which vanishing points are placed in perspective drawing, is called the
questions.explanation: The horizon line represents the viewer's eye level in a perspective drawing, and is where vanishing points are conventionally located.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In orthographic projection, lines projected between related views (such as from the front elevation down to the plan) are called
questions.explanation: Projection lines are thin construction lines used to transfer and align corresponding points and features between the different related orthographic views.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A key advantage of isometric projection over standard orthographic projection is that it
options: always shows the true size of every face equally
eliminates the need for any measurement
shows all three dimensions of an object in a single pictorial view
questions.explanation: Unlike orthographic projection, which requires multiple separate views, isometric projection combines height, width, and depth into one pictorial drawing.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In isometric drawing, the three principal axes are typically arranged at angles of
questions.explanation: The three isometric axes are conventionally spaced 120 degrees apart, giving the characteristic equal visual treatment of all three dimensions.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A significant limitation of one-point perspective compared to two-point perspective is that it
options: is generally less realistic for objects viewed at an angle, since only one set of receding lines converges
cannot represent depth in any way
cannot be used for interior scenes at all
questions.explanation: One-point perspective works well for scenes viewed straight-on, but is less effective for accurately representing objects viewed at an angle, where two-point perspective is more realistic.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A view showing the interior of a solid object after it has been theoretically cut by a plane is called a
questions.explanation: A sectional view reveals the internal structure of an object by depicting it as if cut through by a cutting plane.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The imaginary plane used to theoretically slice through a solid object to reveal its sectional view is called the
questions.explanation: The cutting plane represents the imaginary surface along which a solid is sliced to produce and reveal a sectional view.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A sectional view produced by a cutting plane running parallel to the base of a solid is called a
questions.explanation: A horizontal section results from a cutting plane oriented parallel to the base of the solid being sectioned.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A sectional view produced by a cutting plane running perpendicular to the base of a solid is called a
questions.explanation: A vertical section results from a cutting plane oriented perpendicular to the base of the solid being sectioned.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A sectional view produced by a cutting plane set at an angle other than horizontal or vertical to a solid is called an
questions.explanation: An inclined section results from a cutting plane angled obliquely relative to the solid, neither fully horizontal nor vertical.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When a cone is sectioned by a cutting plane inclined to its base and passing through both slant sides, the resulting true shape of the cut surface is generally an
questions.explanation: Depending on the angle of the cutting plane, sectioning a cone can produce an ellipse, along with other conic sections like parabolas and hyperbolas at different angles.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The true shape of a sectional face, as opposed to its foreshortened appearance in a standard view, is obtained by
options: measuring only the visible outline in the original view
ignoring the angle of the cutting plane entirely
using the plan view directly without further projection
projecting the section onto a plane parallel to the cutting plane
questions.explanation: To reveal the true, undistorted shape of a sectional face, it must be projected onto an auxiliary plane that is parallel to the cutting plane itself.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular solid with a polygonal base and rectangular (or parallelogram) side faces, extending uniformly along its length, is called a
questions.explanation: A prism has two parallel, congruent polygonal bases connected by rectangular or parallelogram-shaped side faces.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular solid with a polygonal base and triangular side faces that converge to a single apex point is called a
questions.explanation: A pyramid has a polygonal base with triangular faces that meet at a single apex point above the base.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular solid with a circular base and a curved surface converging to a single apex point is called a
questions.explanation: A cone has a circular base and a curved lateral surface that tapers uniformly to a single apex point.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A regular solid with two parallel circular bases connected by a uniform curved surface is called a
questions.explanation: A cylinder has two parallel, congruent circular bases connected by a uniform curved lateral surface.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When a cylinder is sectioned by a cutting plane inclined to its axis (but not passing through the base), the resulting true shape of the cut surface is generally an
questions.explanation: Cutting a cylinder at an angle to its axis produces an elliptical sectional shape, unlike a perpendicular cut which yields a circle.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: When a pyramid is sectioned by a cutting plane parallel to its base, the resulting sectional shape is
options: a smaller polygon similar in shape to the base
an irregular shape unrelated to the base
always a triangle regardless of the base shape
questions.explanation: Sectioning a pyramid parallel to its base produces a smaller polygon that is geometrically similar in shape to the original base.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The flat pattern layout showing the true shape of all surfaces of a solid, as if unfolded, is called the
questions.explanation: Surface development lays out the true shape and size of a solid's faces on a flat plane, as if the solid were unfolded or unrolled.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Surface development is particularly useful in industry for applications such as
options: sheet metal fabrication and packaging design
questions.explanation: Development of surfaces provides the flat patterns needed to fabricate objects from sheet metal or cardboard, such as ducts, containers, and packaging.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The part of a cone or pyramid remaining after its upper portion has been cut off by a plane parallel to its base is called a
questions.explanation: A frustum is the remaining lower portion of a cone or pyramid after its top has been sliced off parallel to the base.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The development of a cylinder's curved surface, when unrolled flat, produces a shape that is a
questions.explanation: When unrolled, a cylinder's curved lateral surface forms a rectangle, with one side equal to the circumference of the base and the other equal to the height.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The development of a cone's curved surface, when unrolled flat, produces a shape that is a
questions.explanation: A cone's curved surface, when developed (unrolled), forms a sector of a circle, whose radius equals the cone's slant height.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The development of a prism's side surfaces, when unfolded flat, produces a series of connected
questions.explanation: A prism's lateral faces, being rectangular or parallelogram-shaped, unfold into a connected series of rectangles or parallelograms when developed.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The development of a pyramid's side surfaces, when unfolded flat, produces a series of connected
questions.explanation: A pyramid's triangular lateral faces unfold into a connected series of triangles when the surface is developed.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A key challenge in developing surfaces of intersecting or transitional parts (such as a pipe junction) is determining
options: the number of screws needed for assembly
the true lines of intersection between the different surfaces before laying out the development
the colour scheme to be used
questions.explanation: Accurately developing transitional or intersecting parts requires first establishing the precise lines where the surfaces meet, before the flat pattern can be laid out correctly.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Allowances added to a developed surface pattern for joining edges together, such as folding or seaming, are called
questions.explanation: Seam allowances (or laps) are extra material added to a developed pattern's edges, providing the overlap needed for joining, folding, or seaming the finished piece.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: The part of a building's structure that transfers the load of the building to the ground is called the
questions.explanation: The foundation is the structural base of a building, distributing its weight safely into the supporting ground.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing showing a building's rooms, walls, doors, and windows as seen from directly above, with the roof removed, is called a
questions.explanation: A floor plan is a top-down view of a building's layout, showing the arrangement of rooms, walls, doors, and windows on a given level.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing showing the external appearance of one side (face) of a building is called an
questions.explanation: An elevation depicts the external, vertical face of a building as viewed from one particular direction.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing showing a building's position and layout in relation to its surrounding plot of land is called a
questions.explanation: A site plan illustrates the building's position, orientation, and layout relative to its surrounding land, boundaries, and access routes.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A continuous layer built into a wall near ground level to prevent moisture from rising into the building is called a
questions.explanation: The damp-proof course is a moisture-resistant layer incorporated into a wall to prevent rising dampness from the ground.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A horizontal structural member placed above a door or window opening to support the wall load above it is called a
questions.explanation: A lintel spans across the top of a door or window opening, transferring the load of the wall above safely to the sides of the opening.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A triangular framework of timber or steel members used to support a pitched roof structure is called a
questions.explanation: A roof truss is a triangulated framework designed to support the roof covering and transfer its load down to the walls.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A typical architectural working scale used for building drawings, representing 1 unit on the drawing as 50 units in reality, is written as
questions.explanation: A scale of 1:50 means every 1 unit of measurement on the drawing represents 50 of the same units in real life, a common architectural working scale.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: Standard symbols used on building drawings to represent items such as sinks, toilets, and water pipes are collectively called
questions.explanation: Plumbing symbols are standardised graphic representations used on building drawings to indicate the location of sanitary fittings and pipework.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A threaded cylindrical fastener, typically paired with a nut, used to join mechanical components together, is called a
questions.explanation: A bolt is a threaded fastener designed to be used with a matching nut to securely join mechanical parts.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A small metal piece inserted between a shaft and a hub to prevent relative rotation between them is called a
questions.explanation: A key fits into matching slots (keyways) on a shaft and hub, preventing them from rotating independently of each other.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A wheel with a grooved rim, used with a belt to transmit rotational motion between shafts, is called a
questions.explanation: A pulley, paired with a belt, transmits rotational motion and power between separated shafts.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A wheel with cut teeth, designed to mesh with another toothed wheel to transmit rotational motion, is called a
questions.explanation: A gear has cut teeth that mesh with another gear's teeth, transmitting rotational motion and adjusting speed or torque between shafts.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A cylindrical mechanical component that rotates to transmit power or motion from one part of a machine to another is called a
questions.explanation: A shaft is a rotating cylindrical component used to transmit power and rotational motion within a mechanical assembly.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A mechanical device used to connect two shafts together end-to-end, allowing power transmission between them, is called a
questions.explanation: A coupling joins two separate shafts together, allowing torque and rotational motion to be transmitted from one to the other.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: In mechanical drawing, the acceptable range of variation permitted in a component's manufactured dimension is called the
questions.explanation: Limit tolerances specify the permissible upper and lower boundaries within which a manufactured dimension may vary while still being acceptable.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing showing how individual mechanical parts, such as bolts, nuts, and shafts, fit together as a complete unit is called an
questions.explanation: An assembly drawing illustrates how multiple individual components are combined to form a complete mechanical unit.

questions.subject: Technical Drawing
questions.text: A drawing showing a single mechanical component in isolation, with full dimensions needed for its manufacture, is called a
questions.explanation: A detail drawing focuses on one individual component, providing all the necessary dimensions and specifications for it to be manufactured accurately.
